newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl applauds Germany's Zeiss on 150th anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Kohl applauds Germany's Zeiss on 150th anniversary.

text.p: Germany's Carl Zeiss, famed for the production of high-quality lenses, celebrated its 150th anniversary on Tuesday, applauded as a "model of innovation" by Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

"With the fast translation of scientific discoveries into marketable products the company has always set the standard for the last century and a half," Kohl said at a ceremony to celebrate the firm's 150th birthday in Zeiss's east German home town of Jena.
"Germany should take lessons from this example," Kohl said.
Zeiss, founded in 1846, started out making microscopes and now produces all-kinds of optical equipment, ranging from spectacles to outer space telescopes.
"Innovative products are the prerequisite for the opening up of new markets and the basis for competitive workplaces for the country's future," said Kohl.

But Zeiss said it did not just want to look backwards at its "unrivalled story of strength in innovation," but also to the future. "We are even more committed to leading Zeiss into a healthy business position," said Zeiss board chairman Peter Grassmann.

Although Kohl held up the firm as a paragon, Zeiss has had a difficult couple of years. In the 1995-96 financial year to September 30, Zeiss made a loss of 47 million marks ($31.3 million) on a turnover of 2.65 billion marks.
But the firm, which employs around 13,000 workers, said that it would return to profitability in its anniversary year.
Zeiss was divided into eastern and western concerns after World War Two and the two halves were re-merged in 1990 after the reunification of Germany.
"Few companies have reflected the destiny of Germany as closely as Zeiss," said Kohl.
Almost two-thirds of the jobs in the eastern half were cut and Zeiss completely took over the eastern section in 1995.

But the collaboration between east and west did not go as well as expected and in 1994 the company made a loss of 180 million marks, 140 million marks coming from the Jena-based eastern half, forcing the firm to cut around 3,000 jobs.
Zeiss said losses in the Jena-based business would be reduced in the 1996-97 financial year and that the former eastern concern should be back in the black by 1997-98.

Zeiss said its largest business area remained in optical products with a turnover of 700 million marks, but said its business in semi-conductor optics had grown strongly and had a turnover of 300 million marks in the 1995-96 financial year, that it expected would climb to 350 million marks next year.

Kohl did not just praise the company for its innovation, but also for its respect for the principle of a social market economy, currently under threat in Germany with the souring of relations between workers and employers.
In 1886 the firm introduced a statute, which gave its workers previously unheard-of social rights, including profit sharing and holiday time.
"The founders of Zeiss recognised that business and social responsibility belong together," said Kohl.
